Chapter 2: The First World War—Catastrophe and the Seeds of Upheaval.
When the war first broke out, hardly anyone could truly picture just how devastating it would become. Young men, full of hope and nerves, set off for battle. Crowds cheered them on, certain they'd all be home by Christmas. But as the weeks stretched into months, that optimism slowly faded. Instead, what took its place was sheer horror.
Think about the trenches along the Western Front—muddy, cold, and relentlessly grim. Soldiers huddled close for warmth, swapping stories and holding tight to dreams of peace. Letters from home became their lifeline, little reminders of a world that now felt impossibly far away. The roar of artillery was always in the background, and the threat of death lingered with every sunrise. For those who made it back, the scars ran deep—some you could see, others you couldn’t.
Meanwhile, back home, families waited and worried. Mothers dreaded the knock on the door that might bring terrible news. Kids grew up missing fathers they'd barely known, and whole communities were changed forever by grief. The war didn’t just happen on distant fields—it seeped into daily life, shaping everything from what people ate to how they saw the world.
But the impact went even further. The conflict revealed just how shaky the old political systems had become. Governments were overwhelmed, struggling to keep up with the demands of total war. In Russia, things reached a breaking point. The pressures of fighting, combined with the failures of the Tsarist regime, led to a revolution. The Bolsheviks promised peace and bread, but what followed was civil war and even more hardship.
Around Europe, the collapse of empires brought chaos and opportunity. New states emerged, and nationalist movements surged forward, eager to redraw borders and claim self-determination. But reality wasn’t that simple. Ethnic tensions and old grudges meant that hopes for peace often led to new conflicts instead.
As the fighting dragged on, people grew tired and deeply disillusioned. Those early promises of honor and glory? They’d long since given way to the harsh truth of what war really cost. By the time the guns finally fell silent in 1918, Europe was left mourning. The world everyone once knew was gone—and nobody was quite sure what would come next.
The peace that followed was anything but simple. Treaties like Versailles tried to redraw the map and create a new order, but often just planted the seeds for future trouble. Reparations, shifting borders, and new nations left many feeling betrayed, angry, or just lost. That hope—the hope that this would be the war to end all wars—quickly faded, replaced by a growing sense of dread about what the future might hold.
